description: We are a team of high school students from Liceo TEC Chiquimula, Guatemala, passionate about technology, design and science. Our team combines skills in computer science, graphic design and biology. We want to use what we learn to create simple, useful solutions that help people take care of their health, even in extreme places like space. Our team is complete, and we are excited to learn, create and take part in this challenge.
summary:
During long missions, astronauts lose bone density and muscle mass. They also experience changes in their hearts and eyes, and they have trouble sleeping. In addition, they are far away from doctors. This project presents Star Chance, a web application that allows astronauts to check their health every day.
It includes a three-layer body map (bones, muscles, and organs) that explains each health risk using NASA data. It also has a daily health check that measures heart rate, temperature, blood pressure, and sleep. It compares each result with a reference range and marks it as normal (blue) or needing attention (red). Finally, it creates a report for the flight surgeon.
The application was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and was tested with simulated data. We conclude that this tool allows astronauts to understand their health condition in just a few minutes.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Star Chance is a web app that helps astronauts check their health every day on long missions. It has five views: Home, Body, Check-in, Risks and Sources. In the Body view, the astronaut picks one of three layers of the body (skeletal, muscular or organs) and taps a part: bones, muscles, heart, eyes and brain, or kidneys. Each part shows a NASA figure, a short explanation and its source. The immune system, nutrition and sleep are covered as whole-body topics. The Check-in view asks for four vital signs, one at a time: resting heart rate, body temperature, blood pressure and sleep. Each reading is compared with a cited reference range and marked Normal (blue) or Attention (red). Blood pressure also has a Critical level for a hypertensive crisis. At the end, a summary says All in range, Needs attention or Urgent, and the app prepares a report for the flight surgeon that can be copied or sent (sending is simulated).

What benefits does it have?

It puts health data that is spread across many NASA reports into one simple screen. It explains each risk in the part of the body where it happens. It tells the astronaut which readings need attention and gives them a report ready for the flight surgeon. It runs in any browser, on a computer or a phone, with nothing to install. Every color comes with a written label, so it does not rely on color alone.

What is the intended impact?

On missions to the Moon and Mars, astronauts will be far from a doctor and help from Earth will take longer. Star Chance prepares astronauts to watch their own health, notice changes early and know when to ask for help. It follows the same idea as NASA’s weekly private medical conference between each astronaut and the flight surgeon.

What tools did we use?

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, written in Visual Studio Code. The body drawings and the logo were made in Adobe Illustrator and exported as SVG. GitHub was used for the code and GitHub Pages to publish the app. AI was used to create the base HTML and to summarize and translate part of the NASA information. All the content and the links to official sources were added by hand.

How is our project creative?

Instead of a list of numbers, Star Chance shows health as a map of the body in three layers, so each risk appears where it happens. It turns NASA’s research into a daily routine that an astronaut can follow alone. It also ends with a report for the flight surgeon, so it connects self-monitoring with the medical team.

What factors did our team consider?

Every figure and range must have a cited source (our rule: no source, no data). The app uses simulated data only and does not give medical advice or diagnoses. The reference ranges are for adults on Earth and should be validated by health professionals before using real data. We made it accessible by using labels and not only colors, and kept the language simple. Our team mixed students from computing, graphic design and biology, and each group worked on its own part.
